🧠 Hodgkin–Huxley neuron with stochastic synaptic input

A single-compartment Hodgkin–Huxley (HH) model neuron driven by noisy excitatory and inhibitory synaptic input. Its synaptic conductances are Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes, stepped with the Euler–Maruyama scheme.

How to use

  • Controls (left): every change recomputes the plots and stats live.
  • Random: draw a fresh noise realization at the current settings.
  • Seed: fix the noise for a reproducible run; the active seed is shown under the button.

Model specification

Membrane potential — ||(C_m||) is the membrane capacitance; each ||(E||) is a reversal potential. ||[ C_m \frac{dV}{dt} = I_{ext} - I_{Na} - I_K - I_L - I_{syn} ||]Ionic currents, with gating variables ||(m, h, n||). ||[ I_{Na} = \bar g_{Na}\, m^3 h\,(V - E_{Na}), \qquad I_K = \bar g_K\, n^4\,(V - E_K), \qquad I_L = g_L\,(V - E_L) ||]Synaptic current, where ||(g_E, g_I||) are the excitatory and inhibitory conductances. ||[ I_{syn} = g_E(t)\,(V - E_E) + g_I(t)\,(V - E_I) ||]Gating kinetics — ||(m, h, n||) follow first-order kinetics. ||[ \frac{dm}{dt} = \alpha_m(V)(1 - m) - \beta_m(V)\,m, \qquad \frac{dh}{dt} = \alpha_h(V)(1 - h) - \beta_h(V)\,h, \qquad \frac{dn}{dt} = \alpha_n(V)(1 - n) - \beta_n(V)\,n ||]Synaptic conductances — independent OU processes driven by white noise ||(\xi(t)||). ||[ \tau_E \frac{dg_E}{dt} = (\bar g_E - g_E) + \sigma_E\,\xi_E(t), \qquad \tau_I \frac{dg_I}{dt} = (\bar g_I - g_I) + \sigma_I\,\xi_I(t) ||]Integration — this stochastic differential equation is stepped with the Euler–Maruyama method (stationary variance ||(\sigma^2 \tau / 2||)). ||[ g(t + \Delta t) = g(t) + \frac{\Delta t}{\tau}\big(\bar g - g(t)\big) + \sigma \sqrt{\Delta t}\,\mathcal{N}(0, 1) ||]

🔬 Things to try

  • Draw new noise realizations. Keep every parameter fixed and press Random several times. How much does the spike count change? That spread is trial-to-trial variability caused purely by synaptic noise.
  • Push the neuron across threshold. Raise Iext slowly from 0. At some value the firing switches from sporadic, noise-driven spikes to regular tonic firing — find that transition. Then set sigmaE = sigmaI = 0 to see the sharp, deterministic onset.
  • Balance excitation and inhibition. Increase gE and gI together. Strong E and I can cancel on average while greatly increasing the fluctuations: watch the membrane potential get more jagged even though its mean barely moves.
  • Change the input timescales. tauE and tauI set how long synaptic conductance excursions last: small tau gives fast, uncorrelated noise; large tau gives slow drifts. See how this reshapes the membrane trace.
  • Break the channels. Set gNa = 0 (no spikes) or gK = 0 (no repolarisation) and describe what happens — the classic ablation experiments from the original Hodgkin–Huxley work.
Tip: the active seed under the button identifies the exact noise realization. Note it down to re-create a trace later.
